text: Characterising patients in England with Down syndrome and Alzheimer's disease: a descriptive observational study using data from Clinical Practice Research Datalink linked to Hospital Episode Statistics.

Relationships Among Physical Activity, Functional Fitness, and Cognitive Task Performance in Adults with Down Syndrome. Physical activity (PA) and functional fitness (FF) are associated with cognitive task performance in the general population; however, such relationships remain understudied in adults with Down syndrome (DS). The purpose of this study was to examine associations among moderate-to-vigorous PA (MVPA), FF, and cognitive task performance, and explore whether FF may statistically account for associations between MVPA and cognitive task performance. Thirty-seven adults with DS (35 ± 10 years) completed the Timed-Up-and-Go (TUG) and handgrip strength (HGS) tests to assess FF, and the Eriksen Flanker Task (FT) to assess cognitive task performance. MVPA was measured by an accelerometer device over 7 days. Pearson's correlation indicated that MVPA was significantly associated with TUG (r = -.52, p < .001) and the Flanker effect (r = -.32, p = .047). TUG was associated with FT accuracy (r = -.44, p = .006) and Flanker effect (r = .33, p = .048). Exploratory mediation analysis suggested that TUG performance may partly explain an indirect association between MVPA and FT accuracy, with higher MVPA associated with better FF (i.e. lower TUG time) (β = -.48, p = .003), and better FF was also associated with greater FT accuracy (β = -.52, p = .008). Both MVPA and FF are associated with components of cognitive task performance in adults with DS. Mobility‑related FF showed an exploratory indirect association between MVPA and FT accuracy, suggesting that FF may represent a potential pattern of associations among PA and components of cognitive task performance in this population.

Improving the design of AAC displays: preliminary study of the effects of targeted motion and decluttering on visual attention and symbol learning by individuals with Down syndrome. This study investigates the effects of targeted motion (i.e., smooth movement of a selected AAC symbol from its location to the center of the display) and decluttering of the AAC display on visual fixation duration and accuracy of symbol identification by participants with Down syndrome across three sessions. In each session, participants were first asked to find a target symbol in a grid display with and without targeted motion of selected symbols; data on their visual fixation duration were collected using the Tobii Spectrum Pro. Then they were asked to identify target picture symbols from a unique grid in response to the spoken name of the symbol. Visual fixation duration to target symbols was significantly greater in the condition with targeted motion and decluttering of the display compared to the static display condition across all three sessions. It was difficult for many participants to identify symbols accurately in both of the display conditions; participants demonstrated continued improvements across the three sessions with targeted motion displays while their performance seemed to plateau with the static displays that mimic those used in current practice. Targeted motion may be a powerful tool to increase visual attention to key aspects of AAC displays, but further investigation is required to fully understand how to harness motion to support learning and use of AAC displays.

Metformin improves mitophagy-related pathways and mitochondrial-lysosomal homeostasis in chromosome 21 trisomic fibroblasts. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a core cellular abnormality in Down syndrome (DS), yet the mechanisms underlying impaired mitochondrial quality control remain poorly defined. Here, we provide an integrated characterization of the autophagy-mitophagy-lysosome axis in human trisomic fetal fibroblasts (DS-HFFs). We show that trisomic cells display a paradoxical combination of elevated basal autophagy/mitophagy-related markers and defective mitochondrial clearance, indicative of a saturated and inefficient quality control system. DS-HFFs exhibit increased steady-state levels of PINK1, PARKIN, OPTN, NDP52, LC3-II, and p62, accumulation of autophagic vacuoles, reduced autophagic flux, and impaired delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes. We further demonstrate that metformin alleviates the saturation of the autophagy-mitophagy pathway by modulating multiple components of the mitochondrial quality control pathway, including attenuation of mTOR-associated signaling, enhancement of autophagic flux and normalization of mitophagy-related protein levels. Crucially, metformin increases mitochondria-lysosome association and rescues lysosomal degradative competence as shown by increased Dq-BSA activity, and increased maturation of Cathepsin D. Together, our findings support mitophagy inefficiency due to pathway saturation as a key pathogenetic mechanism in trisomic cells and identify metformin as a pharmacological tool capable of relieving the proteostatic overload intrinsic to trisomy 21. More broadly, these results align with a model in which aneuploidy imposes a chronic proteostatic burden that compromises organelle quality control.

Disseminated BCG disease and recurrent pulmonary infections in a child with trisomy 21 carrying a novel BACH2 variant of uncertain significance: a 5-year case report. Trisomy 21 is associated with combined immune dysregulation, including lymphopenia, impaired responses to vaccines, and heightened susceptibility to respiratory infections, driven in part by triplication of chromosome 21-encoded interferon receptor genes. BACH2 haploinsufficiency is a rare monogenic immunodeficiency characterized by lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, and susceptibility to infections and autoimmune diseases. Co-occurrence of these two conditions has not been previously described.
